blocks.text: **The problem.** Given two integers `n` and `k`, return all possible combinations of `k` numbers chosen from `1` to `n`, in any order.

blocks.alt: Choosing 2 numbers from 1 to 4. From the empty start, take 1, 2 or 3 as the first number; each node then only adds larger numbers, so 12 and 21 can't both appear. The six leaves are 12, 13, 14, 23, 24 and 34. Starting with 4 is pruned: no larger number is left to make a pair.

blocks.text: The idea: a start index keeps one order

A combination is a set, so `[1, 2]` and `[2, 1]` are the same. Building each combination in **increasing order** makes every set appear exactly once: after choosing `x`, only try numbers bigger than `x`. That's the `start` parameter. And there's a cheap but powerful prune: if the path still needs `k − path.length` more numbers, the next choice can be at most `n − (k − path.length) + 1` — anything bigger leaves too few numbers to finish.

blocks.code:
def combine(n, k):
    result, path = [], []

    def build(start):
        if len(path) == k:
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for x in range(start, n + 1):     # only numbers bigger than the last one
            path.append(x)
            build(x + 1)
            path.pop()

    build(1)
    return result

blocks.text: **Time O(C(n, k) · k)** plus dead branches that run out of numbers, **space O(k)**.

blocks.caption: A node never tries a number that leaves too few numbers to finish.

blocks.text: **Time O(C(n, k) · k), space O(k).** Every branch now reaches a real combination, so no work is wasted — a big saving when k is close to n.

blocks.alt: Start index: O(C(n,k) · k) time, O(k) space. With pruning: O(C(n,k) · k) time, O(k) space.
